text:
Every day they went back to the beginning; Adolfo’s passionate nature flared up and grew embittered; the young man would have liked Signora De Carolis to intervene on his behalf, but the mother judged with her daughter’s mind, and could not even remember having reprimanded her once in eighteen years. Indeed, seeing that her daughter was sad, Signora De Carolis too began to think, without having the courage to say so, that Adolfo was brutal; and she regretted having welcomed and encouraged the proposal of the Gianella family, who wanted to unite the two young people. It could not be denied: the peace of the little white house had been disturbed by Adolfo Gianella; Loredana, always cheerful, had changed in character because of him; he, jealous, uneasy, full of suspicion, glared at everyone, did not want them to go to the theater, became irritated by Loredana’s lightheartedness, offended her with incessant remarks, demanded that she already be as serious and prudent as a mother of a family, and finally, even in his good moments, was querulous and tiresome, pedantic and petty.

Because of that ceaseless conflict, the girl was dejected; and more than once Filippo found her with red, swollen eyes.

“You must not marry him, you know,” he would say firmly. “It is an impossible marriage. What will that young man do when he is your husband and has the most foolish and obnoxious rights? Would you like me to speak to your mother?”

The girl did not have the courage to extricate herself from that tormenting situation: the entire Gianella family—Adolfo’s mother, father, uncles, aunts, and cousins—crowded around her, extolling the young man’s virtues, making plans for the future, showing themselves so certain, so delighted about that exceptionally happy marriage, that Loredana stifled herself and kept silent. But no man could have been found who was more incapable than Adolfo of understanding her, so much so that she, kind to everyone, was always irritated, nervous, and distressed with him.

At last he even wanted to read the letters she received from her female friends, whom he did not trust at all; one morning, while he had gone to bid his fiancée good morning, the postman arrived, and Adolfo seized the mail, opened the letter from a girl who was writing to Loredana from a town in the province, asked for information about the people mentioned in it, and ended by putting the letter into his pocket.

When Filippo arrived toward evening, the girl was still trembling all over with indignation and anger; she told her friend everything, even what she had kept silent about until that day: Adolfo’s harassment, stinginess, insulting mistrust, unreasonable jealousy, and conceit.

“I do not want him, I do not want him, I do not want him!” she exclaimed, her eyes blazing with rage. “Anything rather than this marriage! Never, never, never!”

Filippo had listened in silence, looking at the floor of red and white tiles and marking out the rhythm of a march with his foot.

All at once he raised his head, grasped his friend’s hands, and asked:

“Will you come with me?”

The girl did not understand at once.

“Where?” she asked.

“Away, far away, out of Venice, forever!” Filippo pressed.

“Run away? Run away with you?” she said in a low voice, already trembling without knowing why.

“Listen to me,” Filippo murmured.

He went as far as the threshold of the sitting room, saw that her mother was attentively reading a poorly bound book, and continued, returning to Loredana:

“What we call friendship is nothing but love. Have you realized it?”

She, still and rigid, her eyes wide open, did not answer.

“I have realized it,” Filippo went on. “I know that I love you, I feel that I love you, I feel that we can be happy. I cannot marry you; understand me well, I cannot marry you because my whole family would cause us so much grief that, by comparison, what you have suffered until now would seem a joy to you. They are ignorant, stubborn, and ferocious.... But I offer you my love and my life all the same.... I too am weary; I too can no longer drag out this tormented and useless existence. Tell me that you accept, and we shall be happy.... We shall leave at once....”

Loredana withdrew her hands from Filippo’s and stood up: she took a few steps as though to leave the room, but stopped and leaned back against the wall; she was weeping silently, and the tears ran down her cheeks.

Filippo approached her again. He was pale, and his voice trembled. He said:

“Are you offended?”

She shook her head.

“Then you do not love me with romantic love, as I love you?”

No answer came. Loredana looked at her friend through the veil of tears. He took a step as though to move away, but the girl quickly, instinctively detained him with a gesture.

“Yes, I love you too,” she murmured in a low voice.

Filippo seized her around the waist and kissed her on the mouth.

“Think about it,” he said. “Think how happy we shall be.... Your mother will forgive you. She loves you too much to condemn you. She will understand that you had the right to live, to escape a dreadful future. You will know how to make her forgive you, will you not? For you know the road that leads to your mother’s heart! Tell me that you accept, and we shall leave at once....”

She, still leaning against the wall, still motionless, her eyes full of tears, did not answer. But the ringing of the doorbell made both her and Filippo start.

The girl quickly dried her eyes and ran into the sitting room.

“It must be Adolfo,” she said to her mother. “I have a migraine, I do not want to see him, I am going to shut myself in my room!”

Her mother sighed and raised her eyes to the ceiling. Loredana returned to Filippo and clasped his hands while he kissed her on the mouth again.

“Think about it!” Filippo repeated.

She made a vague gesture and disappeared, to shut herself in her little room.

Adolfo Gianella was coming up the stairs, and Filippo, hearing his footsteps, was saying to Signora De Carolis:

“I am very sorry that the young lady is indisposed; I hope it is nothing....”

“Is she ill?” Adolfo asked as he arrived, greeting Filippo with a cold salutation and a sidelong glance. “Where was she last night? She must have caught cold, or eaten something indigestible....”

Filippo left at once, and involuntarily said to himself, laughing inwardly:

“You will soon have to swallow something indigestible yourself!...”

That night he thought again about the idea of running away, which had flashed upon him so suddenly; and the more he thought about it, the better it seemed to him. Signora De Carolis would not have dared do anything against her adored daughter; Adolfo would have found consolation in the thought that a girl capable of running away with Count Vagli was not worthy of him.... Finally, few people would learn of the matter, and only imperfectly, and it would dwindle, be pulverized, so to speak, in the classic Venetian gossip. Filippo found the honesty within his dishonesty; he loved Loredana; he felt that he would be faithful to her, that he would make her happy, that she would not suffer, and since it was absurd to speak of marriage because of the formidable opposition he would encounter in his family, running away—a discreet flight, without too much scandal, without commotion—would put an end to a situation unbearable for him and for his little friend.
